chapter_theme: Moon yoga (சந்திர யோகம்): the body holds the kalas of moon, sun and fire, which with the stars make ninety-six, and the inner moon waxes and wanes as the outer one does. By knowing the fortnights, setting the breaths of sun and moon, joining moon, sun and fire, raising the power from the base through the central channel to the head and keeping bindu, the yogi gains bliss, an unharmed body and freedom from Yama.
structure_note: The kalas are counted first (851 to 860): moon sixteen, sun twelve, fire ten in 852 but sixty-four in 854 to 856, where with four of the stars they total ninety-six, and the nine of elements, lights and star are called the pranava. The middle verses join the three lights and the breaths (861 to 870), then come the serpent and moon (871), a regimen of sleep and food keyed to the moon (872 to 875), and the keeping of bindu, breath and nectar with their fruits (876 to 883). Much of the text is obscure and some lines look corrupt.

851.reading: As the moon's kalas rise and fall through the two fortnights, so the body, pure in its subtle and its gross form, climbs from the subtle into the gross.
851.nuance: மதிக்கலை (the moon's digits) sets the chapter's frame: an inner moon in the body that waxes and wanes like the outer one. How the subtle and gross bodies follow the moon is not explained. A variant reads மதிநிலை for மதிக்கலை.

852.reading: The kalas that arise in moon, sun and fire, sixteen, twelve and ten, all go by the middle way; this is the knowledge known to the yogi who comes to be.
852.nuance: இடைவழி may be 'the middle way' (the central channel) or the இடை (ida) channel. Fire is given ten kalas here, but sixty-four in 854 to 856; the two counts are not reconciled.

853.reading: Sun and moon have kalas that never cease; when fire joins, the unchanging sun takes in all the sixteen kalas of fulfilment through the great breath.
853.nuance: Line 2 (நாறா நலங்கினார் ஞாலங் கவர்க்கொள) I can't construe, and the rest is read only roughly. பெருங்கால் is taken as the great breath.

854.reading: The sun's high kalas are ten and two, the moon's ten and six, and fitting fire's eight eights; examine how they stand.
854.nuance: Twelve, sixteen and sixty-four, stated as sums and products in the manner of the chapter. The verse only counts; what the kalas are is left to the teacher.

855.reading: Fire's kalas are eight eights, the kalas round the sun are counted as twelve, and the moon's are bound at sixteen; these are not merged, yet each is joined with the other.
855.nuance: அனிலின் (of the wind) is read as அனலின் (of fire), to agree with 854 and 856. The last line, distinct yet one with another, is compressed.

856.reading: Fire's sixty-four, the sun's twelve and the moon's sixteen are the kalas, and with the four rays of the stars the kalas bound together number ninety-six.
856.nuance: 64 + 12 + 16 + 4 = 96. Ninety-six is also the number of tattvas in some Tamil Saiva lists, which may be why the total is stated, but the verse does not make that link. A variant reads ஈரெட்டுத் for ஈரெட்டும்.

857.reading: All the kalas run in ida and pingala, and through the unnamed middle channel between them; rousing the base and joining it with the head, the good attain the holy feet and stand there.
857.nuance: இடை, பிங்கலை and the சொல்லா நடுநாடி (the middle channel not named, taken as sushumna) are the three main nadis. மூலம் is the base centre; rousing it to the head is the traditional account of the kundalini's ascent, though the verse does not name the power.

858.reading: In fire, the two small rays, sun and moon, with the star that stays in their play, become the light of the supreme power, which dwells as the nine wheels for the world.
858.nuance: பரையொளி (Para's light) and நவசக்ரம் (nine wheels) are technical; the nine are perhaps those listed in 859. The syntax is loose and the reading is a guess at the joints.

859.reading: Earth, water, fire, air and fitting space, the guarding sun, the rare moon, fire and the contrary star: these nine become the pranava, the great way.
859.nuance: Five elements, three lights and the star make nine, and the nine are said to be Om. The verse names them; it does not say how they make the syllable. முரணிய (contrary, opposed) of the star is unexplained.

860.reading: The star shines in the fortnight when the moon wanes and does not shine in the fortnight when it waxes; the star is all the wombs on earth, and the star within the star is one's own true form.
860.nuance: தாரகை can mean a star, the pupil of the eye, or (as tāraka) the mantra that carries one across, traditionally Om; each fits a different line. The last line, the star of the star as one's own form (சொரூபம்), moves from the sky to the self. தானான்ய் is an encoding slip for தானாம்.

861.reading: In the first fifteen days it sprouts and grows, in the latter fifteen, having grown, it shrinks; for those who can know those fifteen, reaching the feet beyond words becomes possible.
861.nuance: Plainly the moon's two fortnights; in the chapter they are the waxing and waning of the inner moon, which the yogi must learn. The verse does not name what grows and shrinks.

862.reading: Rousing the fire and feeding the rare sun, with the moon that stays the garlands become five and five, and as the senses' going ceases at the swelling star, this is the yoga that joins moon, sun and fire.
862.nuance: தாமம் ஐந்தைந்து (five and five garlands, or abodes) is obscure. The clear claim is the last line: the yoga of the chapter is the joining of the three lights, and it stops the senses' outward going.

863.reading: Though they see the sixteen kalas joined and abiding in the body, the base do not think of it; once harsh Death has set them where he means, they fall into it and their bewilderment does not end.
863.nuance: நீதர் is read as நீசர் (base men). For கருத்துழி (the place he intends) variants give கருக்குழி (the womb's pit), which would make the fall a rebirth, and கழுக்குறி.

864.reading: When fire joins the moon, the sun's light arises; when fire joins the sun, the moon's light; when fire, moon and sun join, that star arises, and what abides there becomes everything.
864.nuance: A symmetrical riddle of the three lights; the joining of all three yields the star, which elsewhere in the chapter is one's own form (860). A variant gives சிவத்தினிற் in the last line, which would place what abides in Siva.

865.reading: Entering without straying, seizing the twelve female kalas and the sixteen male kalas and bringing them, if one pours them into the fire that appears straight ahead, insatiable bliss becomes bliss itself.
865.nuance: Twelve and sixteen are the sun's and moon's counts from 854, but here twelve are called female and sixteen male, the reverse of the common pairing of moon with the female; the verse does not explain. The pouring into fire borrows the language of the fire rite for an inner act.

866.reading: Set the breath of the visible sun on the left and the breath of the great moon on the right; if you do this with care and without error, the axle-pin will not shake for a thousand years.
866.nuance: காலை may be கால் (breath) with the object ending, or 'morning'. The sun's breath usually runs on the right and the moon's on the left, so the verse prescribes a reversal, as tradition reads it. ஆணி (the axle-pin) is taken as the body or life that holds.

867.reading: The nourishing heart resounds with the drum's sound in the nine; there the Supreme of the gods stands as lamplight before what is above, and for the dawn the sun itself is the conch.
867.nuance: The inner sounds heard in yoga are often listed as drum, conch and others. ஒன்பது may be the nine gates or nine sounds. A variant gives பரையோசை (the sound of Para) for பறையோசை (the drum's sound).

868.reading: Sun and moon measure time; within the covering the pouring rain stays; when it thunders and presses beyond the shell of the cosmos, that is the place of the Lord.
868.nuance: பொதிரவன், அதிரவன் and the last line (எதிரவ நீச நிடமது) look like puns on ரவம் (sound) and may be corrupt; ஈசன் இடம் is read from நீச நிடம். The inner rain is often taken as the nectar of yoga and the thunder as nada.

869.reading: No one knows the mantra that meets the light rising from the navel lotus; once they know that mantra, the son is born before the father.
869.nuance: அந்திக்கும் (meets, joins) also echoes அந்தி, the twilight rite. The son born before the father is a riddle of reversal that the verse doesn't solve, and I can't fix whom they stand for. Variants change lines 2 and 3 to 'they did not know by knowledge how it met' and the end to மகன் இருந்தானே (the son was there).

870.reading: Even when they speak they know no gain, and even having recited they are mutes who know nothing; if you can join the beginning and the end, the Lord of the Veda will appear there.
870.nuance: அந்திக்க plays on the twilight worship at dawn and dusk (சந்தி) and an inner joining of beginning and end, perhaps of the breaths or of the moon's course; the verse sets recitation against this inner act. வேதியன் may be the Lord of the Veda or a true Brahmin.

871.reading: The serpent seeks to devour the moon, and the sun's light seeks to burn the serpent; the great one, ending the enmity of serpent and moon and holding them together, will not let them part.
871.nuance: The eclipse serpent swallowing the moon is turned inward: the serpent is traditionally the kundalini and the moon the moon in the head. Line 2 and line 4 (நீண்-கல் கொடானே) are corrupt or obscure, and the variants (துடங்கொளின், கொடானெம்) make the great one either the Lord or the yogi who does this.

872.reading: Not sleeping until what was eaten has settled, sleeping when the practised moon goes down, and carrying within the good fullness, the wondrous fullness reaches the moon.
872.nuance: A regimen of sleep and food. Whether the moon is the outer moon or the inner one, and பூரணை the full moon or the filling of breath, both readings stand. மேவுன்ய் is an encoding slip, read as மேவும்.

873.reading: Not sleeping until the moon rises; when the moon has risen, eating one's food; not sleeping while the moon moves across; and sleeping once the moon has gone down.
873.nuance: The rule is clear in outline, but again the moon may be outer or inner. பிங்கட்டன் in the last line is obscure; a variant reads பிங்கட் டன்றுயில்.

874.reading: Yogis who stay unparted through the aeon measure Yama by the nazhigai; they rise in the world as first of the aeon, and those able to humble themselves become of the moon's hue.
874.nuance: நாழிகையாக நமனை அளப்பர் may mean they count Death's span as a mere nazhigai (twenty-four minutes), or that they hold Death by measured time. Line 4 is corrupt (தாழவல் லார்.க் இச்); a variant reads இன் வழிச் சைவராமே, 'become Saivas of this way'.

875.reading: As the cool moon and the sun move over the earth, one sees the way of earth's and moon's three times; after it ripens on the day the white moon appears, there is not a moment until the cool moon sets.
875.nuance: The verse is too compressed for a firm reading. கணம் இன்று may mean 'not a moment is lost' or 'no moment of waking', continuing 873.

876.reading: Who knows how the six kalas of the growing sun and the six of the waning moon blossom, run twelve finger-breadths, and opening out, fall?
876.nuance: Twelve finger-breadths (பன்னிரண்டு அங்குலம்) is the traditional reach of the out-breath from the nostrils, so the verse is read of the breath, but it does not name it. A variant line 3 (மலர்ந்தேறு பன்னிரண்டோடு எட்டு நாலாம்) changes the count.

877.reading: Though one says the waning moon's day is life's, for the yogi bindu does not go out by its way anywhere; free of desire, it is bound at the base, through awareness of the word set within the moon of Om.
877.nuance: Line 1 and line 4 (ஓமதியத்துள் விட்டு உரையுணர்வாலே) are obscure; ஓமதி may be ஓம் with மதி (moon) or ஓமம் (fire rite). The clear claim is the middle: the yogi's bindu does not leave, because desire is absent and it is held at the base.

878.reading: Joined with the six true kalas of the red sun and the four, the endless one's kalas, with ten, stand closely joined; considered, they pass into the six inner kalas.
878.nuance: Nearly every word is technical or doubtful (சூறுற, ஈறிலி நங்கலை, அகலுவா); the reading only follows the numbers. No firm sense can be fixed.

879.reading: Knowing bindu, in union with the blood, is cast forth, and the united bindu wanes in the rays it casts; if awareness and body stand matched, awareness and body never once leave each other.
879.nuance: சோணி (shonita, the female blood) paired with bindu is the old account of conception. The first two lines are compressed; the last two are clear: when awareness and body are kept in balance they do not part, which is to say death does not come.

880.reading: The unwavering mind, joined with the breath and hooked to the sound of Siva's sounding conch, binds the five senses that no longer drive it: that is release, and they drink nectar, a joy that does not fade.
880.nuance: பவனம் is the breath, and the conch's sound one of the inner nadas. பருகார் may be 'those who drink' or 'they do not drink'; the second would make the last line a reproach to those who do not do this, and both readings stand.

881.reading: On the bank of the river where the nectar-water comes, gathering the five lights in the bubble and driving them through the staff, those able to hold them have no Yama, and their good kalas have no ending day.
881.nuance: தண்டு (the staff) is taken as the spine and its central channel, and the nectar as what flows from the moon in the head. குமிழி (the bubble) and the five lights are not explained. The line is garbled in the text (தண்டோ ட்டி, நமன்இகில்லை, நாளனஇல்லை).

882.reading: Opening the spring of nectar-water within and sending the clear water to the lotus of the two feet, settled in the samadhi of clear water, unending good goes on by the eye's stream and the breath's course changes.
882.nuance: இணையடித் தாமரை (the lotus of the two feet) is the Lord's feet, here perhaps placed in the head. கண்ணாற்றொடே (by the eye's stream) is obscure; கால்வழி மாறும் is read as the breath's course changing, as in yogic stilling of the breath.

883.reading: If the moon and its partner, unchanging and without disorder, reach the head by the staff, the body comes to no harm, the means one seeks is won, and a joy that does not decay wells up on earth.
883.nuance: The variant மதியும் ஆதித்தனும் மாறின்றி (moon and sun without exchange) makes the partner the sun; the printed line (மதித்திரு) is unclear. The end, joy here on earth (பார்மிசை), not only after death, fits the tantra's aim of a perfected body.

links.note: 1936 faults people who do not know how bindu is lost or how to guard it; 877 describes the yogi in whom bindu does not go out, held at the base for want of desire.
724 says that if the body perishes life perishes, so Tirumular learned to nourish the body; 879 gives the condition for their not parting: awareness and body kept in balance.
Both use the moon's two fortnights: the Kural for friendship with the good that fills and with fools that wanes, Tirumular for the inner moon whose growing and shrinking the yogi must learn.

Both use the eclipse serpent that seizes the moon: the Naladiyar's spares the young crescent, as the worthy spare a fallen enemy; Tirumular's enmity of serpent and moon is ended and the two held together, an inner joining.

851 says the body climbs and descends (ஏறி இறங்கும்) like the moon's kalas through the two fortnights (இருவகைப் பக்கத்துள்). 793 says moon and sun, alternating over the two fortnights, rise and fall (ஏறி இழியும்) through ida and pingala, with life welling between them. 793 names the channels in which 851's waxing and waning happen.

852 gives fire ten kalas beside the moon's sixteen and the sun's twelve (ஈரெட்டு ஆறிரண்டு ஈரைந்து). 854 gives fire eight eights, sixty-four (அங்கியது எட்டெட்டு உயர்க்கலை), and 855 and 856 repeat that count. Read as counts of the same thing, the two numbers for fire's kalas conflict; the tension disappears only if ஈரைந்து in 852 counts something other than fire's kalas, which the verse does not say.

859 says the nine, five elements, three lights and the star, become the pranava, the great way (பிரணவமாகும் பெருநெறி). 227 says the faultless Brahmins grasp the pranava that is the great way (பெருநெறியான பிரணவம்). Both verses call Om the பெருநெறி; 859 builds it from the elements and lights, 227 makes it the Brahmin's discipline.

860 ends that the star within the star is one's own form (தாரகைத் தாரகை தானாம் சொரூபமே). 2574 sets the teaching of Om in the bliss of one's own form (சொருபானந்தம்) in turiya. The pairing holds on the reading of தாரகை as tāraka, the saving syllable Om; on that reading 2574 says what 860 points at.

862 says rousing the fire (அங்கி எழுப்பி) and feeding the sun, with the moon, ends the senses' outward going: the yoga that joins moon, sun and fire. Thiruppugazh 506 asks when, from the fire in the root lotus (மூலகமலத்து இலங்கியை), driven through the nadis to join the moon (இந்துவின் ஊடுற இணக்கி), he will drink the nectar. The song turns 862's instruction into a prayer for the same ascent.

863 says the base see the sixteen kalas in the body and do not think of it, until harsh Death sets them where he intends (கன்றிய காலன் கருத்துழி வைத்தபின்) and they fall. Naladiyar 331 compares those who revel in the world while great Death waits to seize them (கொலைவல் பெருங்கூற்றம் கோள்பார்ப்ப) to a turtle playing in a pot over the fire. Both make the fault not seeing what is plain while Death prepares; Tirumular names the unheeded thing as the inner kalas.

864 says that when fire, moon and sun join (அங்கி சசிகதிர் கூட), the star arises and what abides there becomes everything (சகலமுமாமே). 1990, in another chapter, says that when the sun joins fire and moon (அருக்கன் அனல்மதியோடு ஒன்ற), that is the fullness (பூரணை). Both make the union of the three lights the point of completion.

866 prescribes setting the sun's breath on the left and the moon's on the right so that the axle-pin will not shake for a thousand years (ஆணி கலங்காது அவ் ஆயிரத்தாண்டே). Thiruppugazh 355 prays not to become a foolish yogi who, thinking this impermanent flesh will last (அனித்தமான ஊன் நாளும் இருப்பதாகவே), holds the breath in the nostrils. The one teaches breath-craft for a lasting body; the other names that very aim a delusion.

866 makes the goal of breath-craft that the axle-pin should not shake (ஆணி கலங்காது). 309 says that even when the axle turns and the pin is shaken (அச்சு உழன்று ஆணி கலங்கினும), the First comes near only to those who know him with longing. Read with the pin as the body's hold on life, 309 limits 866: a steady pin is not what brings the Lord near.

867 says the heart resounds with the drum's sound (பறையோசை) in the nine and the sun is the conch (சங்கு) at dawn, with the Supreme standing as a lamp. 606 lists the ten inner sounds, among them conch and drum (வளை பேரி), and says only those who have bowed can perceive them. 606 places 867's drum and conch in the full list of inner nadas and adds the condition for hearing them.

869 says that once the mantra meeting the light from the navel lotus is known, the son is born before the father (தந்தைக்கு முன்னே மகன் பிறந்தானே). 1026 says the six-faced one appears before his father (தந்தைதன் முன்னே சண்முகம் தோன்றலால்) and is to be held as the son. The same reversal of son before father appears in both; 1026 names the son as Skanda, which offers one key to 869's unsolved riddle.

870 calls those who recite yet know nothing mutes (ஓதியும் ஏதும் அறியாத ஊமர்கள்), and says the Lord appears only to those who can join beginning and end. Kural 834 says there is no greater fool than one who studies, understands and teaches but does not restrain himself (ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் பிறர்க்குரைத்தும் தானடங்கா). Both judge recitation empty without an inner act; the Kural names it self-restraint, Tirumular an inner yogic joining.

872 says not to sleep until what was eaten has settled (அயின்றது வீழ்வளவும் துயிலின்றி). Kural 942 says the body needs no medicine if one eats only after what was eaten is digested (அருந்தியது அற்றது போற்றி உணின்). Both time the next act by the settling of the last meal; the Kural applies it to eating, the Tirumanthiram to sleep, within its moon regimen.

Kural 334 says what shows itself as a day is a blade that saws through life (நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி உயிர் ஈரும் வாள்). 874 says yogis who stay through the aeon measure Yama by the nazhigai (நாழிகையாக நமனை அளப்பர்). On the reading that they count Death's span as a mere nazhigai, the yogi measures time rather than being cut by it, against the Kural's claim that time cuts every life.

876 asks who knows how the kalas of sun and moon blossom, run twelve finger-breadths (பன்னிரண்டு அங்குலம் ஓடி) and fall. 2764 says to seek where the life-breath rises and runs twelve finger-breadths (பன்னிரண்டு அங்குலம் ஓடும் உயிர்): that is the hall where the Lord of nada's end dances. 2764 answers 876's question with a place and its meaning.

879 says that if awareness and body stand matched, they never once leave each other (உணர்வும் உடம்பும் ஒருகால் விடாவே). 2148 says people cling to body after body without knowing the bond between body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு அறியாதார்). 879 states the bond 2148 says people miss, and how it is kept.

880 says the mind joined with the breath binds the five senses (ஐம்புலன் கட்டுண்ணும்) and that is release (வீடு). Naladiyar 59 says one who can guard, without wavering, the craving that enters through the five gates of body, mouth, eyes, nose and ears will surely reach release (வீடு பெறும்). Both make holding the five senses the way to வீடு; 880 does it by breath and inner sound, the Naladiyar by firm guarding.

880 hooks the mind to the sound of Siva's conch (சிவசங்கின் நாதம்) and ends with drinking nectar (அமுதமே). Thiruppugazh 506 asks for the conch-sounding bindu-nada (சங்கொலி விந்துநாதம்) at the front and then to drink the gods' nectar (வானவமுதத்தை உண்டு). The same sequence, inner conch-sound then nectar, appears in both.

881 says that those who gather the five lights and drive them through the staff on the bank of the nectar river have no Yama (நமன் இல்லை). 622 says that once the upper door at the summit of the root channel is seen open, Death's word does not reach one even in dreams (காலன் வார்த்தை கனாவிலும் இல்லையே). Both promise freedom from Death to the one who carries the ascent through the central channel to the top.

882 is a near-repeat of 336: both open with 'opening the spring of the inner water's nectar' (உண்ணீர் அமுதமுறும் ஊறலைத் திறந்து), turn to the lotus feet (இணையடித் தாமரை), samadhi, and end with the eye's stream and the breath's way (கண்ணாற்றொடே சென்று கால்வழி). In 336 the feet are the guru's and the breath's way is seen (காணுமே); in 882 the clear water is sent to the feet and the breath's way changes (மாறுமே).

724 says that if the body perishes life perishes and true knowledge cannot be reached, so he learned to nurture the body. 883 says that when moon and its partner reach the head by the staff, the body comes to no harm (ஊறு படாது உடல்) and undecaying joy wells up on earth (பாறுபடா இன்பம் பார்மிசை பொங்குமே). 883 gives the fruit of the nurture 724 argues for: joy here, in the kept body.

source_issues: 860 line 4 (தானான்ய்) and 872 line 4 (மேவுன்ய்) have encoding slips, read as தானாம் and மேவும்.
871 line 4 (நீண்-கல் கொடானே), 874 line 4 (தாழவல் லார்.க் இச்) and 881 lines 3 to 4 (தண்டோ ட்டி, நமன்இகில்லை, நாளனஇல்லை) are garbled in the text.
855: அனிலின் (of the wind) is read as அனலின் (of fire), to agree with 854 and 856.
852 gives fire ten kalas, while 854 to 856 give sixty-four.
853 line 2 and 868 line 4 are obscure and may be corrupt.
863: variants கருக்குழி and கழுக்குறி for கருத்துழி; 869: variants change lines 2 to 4; 883: variant மதியும் ஆதித்தனும் for the unclear மதித்திரு. Each changes the sense.
